1930: The propeller's ceiling. The last great piston designs were already brushing the sound barrier in dives, before anyone had the math to explain what was happening.
1940: The jet shock. Turbines arrived mid-war, experiments went supersonic, and everything about air combat had to be rethought inside a decade.
1950: Altitude as armor. Bombers, transports and spyplanes bet that flying higher and longer beat flying faster. For a decade, it worked.
1960: The Mach 3 bet. Steel, titanium and folding wingtips chased raw speed, right up until surface-to-air missiles made the bet obsolete.
1970: Agility replaces speed. Swing wings, titanium bathtubs and deliberately compromised top speeds. The lesson of the 60s, absorbed.
1980: The disappearing act. A Soviet math paper and forty years of flying-wing stubbornness turned stealth from theory into hardware.
1990: Stealth learns to fight. The first airframe asked to hide from radar and win a dogfight at the same time.
2000: One airframe, every job. Three services, three ways to land, one production line.
2020: The bet doubles down. The flying wing is no longer the exception. It is the plan for the entire bomber fleet.
